prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, taking timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I ranked IceCube first and the lattice clock second, but after reading the ballots I move B012 to the top of my configuration. It is the only candidate that seven of eight members ranked, and the reason holds up on the science rather than on counting votes. The magic-wavelength idea (Katori) removes the lattice light shift while keeping thousands of atoms, and the group at JILA (Ye) pushed the systematics and stability to roughly 1e-18. Several independent laboratories now reproduce and compare such clocks over fibre links, and clocks are measuring the gravitational redshift across millimetres. As an instrument builder I recognise the patient calibration and systematics work behind that number. The attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: two named people, both of whom every member who ranked the candidate proposed, with the concept and the performance frontier each clearly owned. The physics will last, because the clocks are the basis for the planned redefinition of the second and for searches for varying constants and dark matter.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and credit breadth. The 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (ion control) cover neighbouring ground, ion clocks reach similar accuracy, and Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others were essential to making lattice clocks work. A two-name prize necessarily leaves out parts of a wide community. There is also a fair argument that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened and the promised applications (geodesy, dark-matter searches) are still being realised. Against my own first choice, IceCube, the case against is that the diffuse flux is firmly established but only a few sources are identified, and credit is spread over Baikal, AMANDA and a very large collaboration.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the lattice clock only fifth and suggests the committee might wait for the redefinition of the second, with overlap against frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I do not think a prize should wait for the redefinition. The criterion is the demonstrated discovery or invention, and 1e-18 uncertainties agreeing across independent laboratories already exist. The redefinition is a metrology decision that would follow the science, not validate it. I accept the overlap point in part: the comb prize gave the ruler and the ion prize gave single-system control, whereas the lattice clock is a distinct step that combines many atoms with Lamb-Dicke confinement, so it is not a repeat. Your own first choice, B021, is a fine instrument achievement, but it has no support beyond you in the opening ballots and the STEM corrector priority issue you raise is a real problem.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a surprise from experiment with a quantitative theory-experiment link, and the clock only fifth.
responses.response: I agree that B036 is a genuinely new platform and the theory-plus-experiment pairing is attractive, but I share the doubts both you and Mehlig note: the experimental discovery is about eight years old, the pairing mechanism is still debated, and Cao, Fatemi and others in the original work are outside the credited names. I would rather wait for the interpretation to settle than award a field that is still moving. By contrast, the lattice clock result is reproduced at its stated precision by several groups, so I see it as the more secure choice this year, with B036 a strong candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery first and IceCube second, arguing that the experimental discovery of the Higgs is overdue and fairly represented by a few spokespeople.
responses.response: I rank B039 fifth, not because the discovery is in doubt, but because of attribution. Two experiments of several thousand people each, and four plausible names of which at most three can be chosen, means any trio will leave out people whose work on detectors, triggers and calibration was decisive. I made the same choice differently from you (I put Della Negra in place of Jenni), which shows how contestable it is. I share your support for IceCube, but I now think it is a candidate for a later year, as the sources beyond TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane are still few.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a clean universal mechanism confirmed in HgTe, with twisted bilayer graphene and cold-atom Hubbard simulation next.
responses.response: I ranked B057 only seventh, and your own attribution note is the reason: the HgTe realisation was predicted by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not in the credited trio, so a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp prize rewards the Z2 idea and the experiment but leaves a hole in the middle. I also see the 2016 prize as covering much of the topological ground, though I am relying on you and Eriksson for the condensed-matter judgement. I would keep B057 as a serious alternative if the committee can settle the credit, but I do not think it beats the lattice clock on clarity.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, a clean discovery and enabling platform, and the lattice clock fifth.
responses.response: I take the quality of B051 seriously, but I share your own worry that the 2025 prize recognised superconducting circuits only one year ago, and the committee may not want to reward the same platform again so soon. It also rests more on a platform for applications than a measurement of nature, and I defer to you, Kroll and Lindroth on the atomic and quantum-optics side. I would ask you whether the lattice clock's fifth rank in your ballot reflects a scientific reservation or just priority among many strong candidates.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a two-person prize is fair to Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and other lattice-clock contributors, and whether any of them should be added.
Whether the expected redefinition of the second should affect timing.
Whether IceCube credit (Halzen, Karle, Spiering versus Baikal and AMANDA founders) can be settled for a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B012 is apparent from my profile. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, none of which are involved in lattice clocks. For B029 (IceCube), my field is close to neutrino astronomy and multimessenger work, and Fermi-LAT took part in follow-up of the TXS 0506+056 alert, so I would flag a mild proximity, but no personal tie to the credited names is apparent.
